title: The Center of All Existence
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The talk's main teaching is that our true purpose and passion can be found by listening to an inner call or essence that guides us, but this requires letting go of ego and control. By trusting this inner voice and embracing the present moment with all its uncertainties, we can find comfort and growth in not knowing what's next. This involves cultivating a sense of curiosity, openness, and willingness to risk, allowing life to unfold without obstruction or control.

Oh my goodness, what fool would ever leave this place?
Goings and goings tonight, huh?
And there was a, was it a house sparrow that was singing with us?
It was a white house sparrow.
Thank you.
Wasn't that wonderful?
Two of them just lit up there and sang along with us.
So I wrote a little something, that's not, this is a big something, in the newsletter, but to say thank you.

I don't know that I'm going very far for very long, but it's a good opportunity to reflect on my good fortune to have practiced with you, to have arrived up here and been welcomed by all of you, by Nancy.
She was not around very much, but I remember her warmth enormously when I first arrived.
To take stock and to talk a little bit about this time of transition in my life.
And it calls forth one of my favorite topics, which is that impulse that causes us to seek.
The title of this talk is something like the center of all existence.
I love that.
I actually think it's the title of a category talk somewhere, but it seems to fit perfectly here.
Not long ago we saw our first image of the black hole.
Did you see that?
Yeah.

I just thought it was absolutely wonderful that one of the main people that made those images possible was a woman, an MIT PhD named Katie Bowman, who began working on the algorithm that was necessary to generate this image when she was working on her PhD at MIT.
She's the one who created that.

And I thought, what is it that lets someone know at some point early in their life that they have a passion, that they're going to apply all of their energy towards to create and find something that's never been found before?
What is that in us, in each of us, in each of you, that passion?
She predicted the white halo of light around it, and it was really there.
And I think in a way that's a metaphor for us.
In that center of the black hole, time and space don't exist.
You might say that it's the still point of all existence.
It's what it's like in the middle of our zazen when we're really sitting, letting go of thoughts.
When we drop away body and mind, what's there?
What is there?
What?
Everything meets this moment, and poof, something happens.
Sometimes we call it an appropriate response, enlightened activity, bodhisattva manifestation.
Sometimes we call it a mess, but never a mistake.
Poof, and something happens again.
We show up as a part of it.
We, that is, me or you, this body in this form, alive in this moment, moment by moment, living out this life of Andrea or Ben or Hannah.
It's a Zen idea or ideal to live our life in a zone like that.
How does that happen?

Many years ago now, it seems, one of my close Dharma sisters in Berkeley and I were talking, and she asked me, "Have you ever wondered why the green grass grows up through the cracks in the concrete?"
Karen started practicing when she was a teenager, and she's my age, so that was a long time ago.
That was a very profound question to her.
It's a very profound question.

She was thinking about her mother, who at that point, her name was on our altar, Kathy Sondheim finally has passed on, but somehow her mother, who was in many ways emotionally miserable, she had arthritis, she lived in pain, she kept going.
She was miserable.
She fell, broke her hip, she had confusion, but still she kept going.
She kept going, like grass growing through the sidewalk.
My life work, it seems, has been as a geriatrician.
People come to see me who can no longer do what they used to do, and they don't feel like who they know themselves to be.
Like they've lost themselves, and our work together is to rediscover the essence of what their life is in this new form.
What is it that keeps the green grass of their life growing?
How does your life manifest?
How does it take its different forms?
There are interests that we pursue, people we associate with, what we do for livelihood and recreation.
Do we marry?
Do we have children?
Do we like cats or dogs?
Do we show up for friends when they're in trouble?
Do we forgive our parents for whatever it was that they did?
Do we move on through adversity or get thrown back on our heels?
How do we keep poking our heads up through the muck and the concrete obstacles in our lives and keep turning toward our mission?
To grow toward the sun and live out our lives productively.
To touch back into that root core of who we are despite and because of all the circumstances.
We say that there are moments when our lives are most alive.
What are those moments?
The title of this talk might also be the five factors of manifesting life.
I chewed on Karen's question for some time.
I gave a Dharma talk on it a long time ago in Milwaukee.
It's still an interesting question to me.
What's the quality of this green grass growing, the spark of our lives?
I'm going to tell you my five factors that I've come to at this point.
The first is to recognize and trust your inner call.
That inner call or seed, it's your essence.
It's the essence core of who, what makes you, you.
It's that essence that even when you're 70, 80, 90 years old, no matter what shape your body is in, no matter what limitations you have, that core is still always going to be with you.
You'll always be able to find it if you're willing to be curious and look for it.
Do you know what it is right now?
How would you define it for yourself right now?
Sometimes we see it as a talent or a tendency that gives you a spark.
If you're lucky when you're young, you recognize it.
If you're lucky, maybe a teacher or a parent, maybe your second cousin sees it in you and somehow points it out.
Maybe it's a light that runs in your family or maybe it's something that happens early on in your life.
If your antennas are tuned in, you get it when you're young.

Sometimes it takes us a very long time to find it or to remember what it was, that incident when you were nine and walking down the street, your mother said about the nuns that that was a holy life, but sometime later you find that you were one of those too and in fact it was the life you were meant to live.
If you're lay ordained, your teacher will give you a name that perhaps points to that essence.
Maybe it won't even seem familiar to you at first, but you keep turning it over and over and maybe it does.
And our job is to respond to it.
Sometimes we have doubt.
Our job is to respond to it.
This is like, why am I going now?
Sometimes you know something's out of place.
Sometimes you know that life needs to bloom or blossom in some other place.
You don't quite understand it, but you just know something needs to shift.
Sometimes it's a curiosity.
Sometimes it's clear and direct like moving towards bright light, like a moth that just can't resist.
Sometimes you take your job and run off to join the circus. [unclear: "No, the runoff."] Kind of like that.
It functions as intuition.
The definition of intuition is the ability to understand something immediately and without conscious reasoning.
Actually, one of the reasons, when Suzuki Roshi was asked why we practice Zen, he gave a hundred different answers.
So I can say one of the reasons we practice Zen is to be able to touch into our intuition.
To know without this getting in the way.
You just know.
Sometimes it's a ha ha.
Sometimes you know where to move towards and sometimes you just know that something needs to change.
Sometimes it's a creeping realization or a disquietude that it's time to move.
The snow's melting and it's time to rouse from hibernation.
Freud, for whomever we see him now, was an early promoter of the workings of the subconscious.
And he said in the major decisions of your life, it wasn't trying to understand [unclear: "the it"] or the ego.
In those major decisions like marriage or career, it was go with your gut.
Gut is like that alarm clock of the seed that tells you when it's time to sprout or turns the embryo on to grow.
It's not always that easy, though, is it?
We have a mind that can get in the way.
There's the hindrances, anxiety, fear, hatred can so overwhelm it that we miss it.
Sometimes those things, though, are part of the reason that we come to practice.
Sometimes we lose track of that place.
We get distracted, overwhelmed, lost by our lives, just caught up in our responsibilities.
Just overwhelmed by the events of the world.
That's hindering doubt.
Hindering doubt is when we lose our track.
It's not the same as the questioning doubt.
The questioning doubt is what turns the light on and says, go look, go look.
Questioning doubt inspires action and the impulse to understand can, in fact, be helpful for mindfulness practice.
A questioning attitude encourages deeper investigation.
It's a healthy doubt that can overcome complacency and loosen preconceived ideas if you're willing to take the risk.
Doubt might also be seen as curiosity, to take whatever we think is happening or assessment as provisional.
I don't know.
I don't know.
I honestly don't know what I'm doing.
But there's some question, and I'm just going to take it as provisional.
What else is there?
This moment, this thought, this impulse, this arising, keep moving.
Factor number one, recognize and trust your inner call.
Factor number two is trust your life.
I think that's a hard one, actually.
Trusting our lives, that it's enough, that nothing's out of place.
And related to that is that every moment is your necessary Dharma position.
So Dharma position is a Buddhist term.
It means what happens, how you manifest in this moment at any one given point in time.
And I was reminded of that recently as one of my friends came to visit.
This man grew up in Philadelphia but had roots in Texas and a very religious family.
And he was gay and closeted and it was quite difficult for him.
He turned to drugs.
He really almost got in big time trouble several times over, almost lost his life.
Kind of turned himself around, came out, continued to struggle, then he got cancer.
And he survived cancer.
And Jeff is one of the most loving, generous, if you need him, he'll be there for you people.
And I recognized in our visit that every single experience of his life was necessary to make him who he is.
That's our lives too.
Every single experience is necessary to bring you to the Zen-Do right now, right this moment, to wake up.
Trust your life.
Every moment is a necessary Dharma position.
It's not what we think our lives should be.
We don't need to fix things.
Perhaps we have regrets or shame.
Maybe we do need to change things or address things.
I wouldn't be here if I hadn't had regret and shame about my actions.
Maybe we change.
Maybe those conditioned tendencies continue to present themselves.
I promise you they always will.
Sometimes they trip us up, surprise and disappoint us, pick ourselves up.
We keep going on.
It's all part of the stew of our lives.
It's Genjokoan, that is, on the question of finding our way in the moment of our circumstances.
Every part of our lives is essential to ourselves, an organic manifestation of our genetics, psychology, experiences, and yes, our cultivation.
Buddha, if we were quoting him in the Pali Canon, might say something like, "Just as a plant that is well-tended, fertilized, pruned, and water will flourish and bear fruit, so is it with our lives."
So cultivation is essential.
As I like to say, our vow, our beacon, our direction is the precept practice on a daily basis.
Trust Your Life, Part Two: life is fully functioning when you aren't in the way.
We have this big question about our lives, what the meaning of it is and what I will do.
And that brings me to one of my two favorite Zen koans, and you're going to get both of them in this talk.
Dao Wu asked, "What is the fundamental meaning of Buddha Dharma?"
Most of you know this one.
Shi Tao said, "Not to attain, not to know."
Pretty snappy answer.
Dao Wu said, "Can you say anything further?"
Like, "I don't get it.
Explain that to me."
And Shi Tao said, "The vast sky does not hinder the white clouds from flying."

The vast sky: our unencumbered mind, the mind that doesn't have obstacles, the mind that doesn't have hindering doubts, the mind that's not obscured by greed, hate, and delusion, the mind that's in the center of all existence, in the middle of that black hole.
That mind is big sky.
And the white clouds, the thoughts that come and go, the ones of our hurried and flurried lives, they just keep moving on when we don't grab onto them.
It is in this place, where we sit in the blue sky and the white clouds just keep passing by, that intuition can arise.
Suzuki Roshi adds, "Not gaining and not knowing, we try not to control the moving because we are a part of it."
There's no way to objectively observe the total movement because we are a part of it, even though we try to control, observe, or hinder the moving to our liking.
So it's all just functioning despite us.
Within the interconnectedness, we are one musician within the symphony.
We are a part of the music.
We cannot be the observer or the audience, otherwise we disturb or destroy the music.
We are already completely and totally participating.
Trust your life because we are a part of it.
You can't separate yourself out except by your ideas.
Our job, so to speak, is to take our place in that symphony.
We may be the conductor, the oboist, or maybe only at one moment do we strike the cymbals.
I doubt the grass thinks of itself as apart from soil, clouds, or rain.
Why should we?
Of course, who knows?
But then, the roots of trees and the larger biome communicate.
Mirror neurons exert their influence even now as we sit here together in this space.
Right now, one heart, one mind beating in our independent thoughts.
So point two is trust your life.
Point three is be willing to risk.
It will turn out all right.
It may be hard to believe, especially in your own experience, because not all of us have had easy lives.
Maybe it won't be the job you thought, the house.
What is it that can really be relied upon?
Maybe the circumstances will just be unimaginable.
Somehow you'll meet them.
Somehow, from your center, from your core, you'll be able to meet them.
Those who survived are not attached to one thing.
They're flexible and creative.
I think often of Suzuki Roshi's example during the war, when all the [unclear: "others and priests"] were finding jobs because they didn't know how they were going to be able to feed their families.
And he said, "I'm going to run an experiment.
I'm going to see if the Buddha Dharma really works or not.
I'm going to fullheartedly give myself to the Buddha Dharma and see what happens."
And so he started a garden, planted a few vegetables, started to be able to grow a few things.
People came.
They needed the food.
They brought what they had.
Before he knew it, the rice coffers were filled.
He gave them away.
They filled up again.
People came and practiced together.
He just genuinely offered his best knowledge of practice, and somehow that little community flourished.
Suzuki needed to take a job as a teacher or something else.
Be willing to risk.
Don't know.
I counted five factors, but I divided some of them.
This is actually five now: don't know.

When I came to Tassajara for the first time, which was a long time ago, I'd given up my well-paid and somewhat prestigious job on a semi-academic track on the basis of a program announcement about a Buddhist program.
I had no idea what I was doing.
Somehow my true teacher was there, although I didn't think she was at the time.
I found myself at Tassajara less than a year after she died, and I went into the abyss with the exhilaration of being there.
I plopped myself down, and I said, "I have no idea why I'm here."
I meant it.
I just knew I had to be there.
She said to me, my second favorite Zen story, which many of you know, she told the story of Dizon and Fayon.
Dizon was on pilgrimage.
He was on pilgrimage, by some stories, with a bunch of his other friends.
They got stuck in a snowstorm, so they had to make a detour unexpectedly.
Here he is on pilgrimage.
Not only is he wandering and looking for truth somewhere, but now he's completely lost, and he winds up at this strange monastery.
He asks the abbot of that temple.
He says, oh, I'm sorry.
This is Fayon, who's on pilgrimage.
He asked Dizon, who's the abbot.
Yeah, Dizon, the abbot, asked Fayon, "Where are you going?"
And Fayon says, "Around, on pilgrimage."
And Dizon said, "What's the purpose of pilgrimage?"
And Fayon said, "I don't know."
And Dizon said, "Not knowing is most intimate."
Not knowing is most intimate.
Intimate means closely acquainted, familiar, close, welcoming, or hospitable.
It points to a very close connection.
It's odd to think that not knowing is intimate when it's supposed to be familiar, close, and you're searching for it, isn't it?
Maybe it's welcoming and hospitable because you recognize it when you feel it.
I like the definition that says it's private and personal.
It's not known even to ourselves.
Not known even to ourselves, but there it is operating.
There it is operating.
The big sky cannot obstruct the white clouds from flying.
That's what we do when we sit, like the river flowing out in the dark and the arrow points meeting in midair.
Dizon's poem says:
*Let it be short, let it be long.
Stop cutting and patching.*
Don't try to control it.
*Going along with the high, along with the low, it levels itself.*
No matter what the circumstance, you can trust it.
It'll be all right.
The abundance or scarcity of the house is used according to the occasion.
You'll have what you need.
It'll be all right.
*Roaming serenely in the land, she goes where her feet take her.*
Not knowing creates.
There is no good or bad, no want or dislike, no obstruction.
There's wonder and curiosity.
Not knowing creates potential, aliveness.
It creates space for life to occur, not limited by our ideas.
It's the center of all existence.
Grass grows through the cracks in the sidewalk.
Life has its own force.
Birds nest in a dark hole that they can see.
Trust how your life is called.
The next breath arises.
Life takes care of itself if we get out of the way.
We get up to do the next thing, be willing to risk, effortlessly, without even knowing why or how it appears.
Grass grows through cracks in the sidewalk.
Birds nest in a dark hole that they see.
The next breath arises.
We get up to do the next thing effortlessly.
Maybe I'll stop there and see if you have any questions, comments, thoughts.
What's your experience?
Five points are: know that inner voice.
Trust your life.
Every moment is necessary.
Life is fully functioning when you aren't in the way.
And don't know, be willing to risk.
How's that land?
Do you agree with it?
Do you have an experience of it?
**Participant:** I agree with it.
When I listen to it, it makes me really come alive.
There's a great sense of vulnerability when I hear parts of it.
Even excitement meets, I'm scared.
Maybe even scared.
So it makes me really come alive.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** What do you do when the fear arises?
**Participant:** I haven't had any horrible things happen in my life.
It sounds good, but I wonder if someone's been to war or they've had children die or the horrible things of life.
I think it would be really hard to say I trust life.
It would certainly shape you and make you who you are.
That would be a whole different thing than a life like mine, if you haven't had too many bad things happen.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** I think that's really a key question.
What does that exactly mean?
What I'm trying to point to is, in a small way, aging encapsulates all of it, because you're falling apart and you're going to die.
It's pretty scary.
But if you have some sense of where your power is, where your center is, that you can touch into that despite the circumstances.
It doesn't mean that I trust everything that goes on around me.
It doesn't mean that I trust that systems are looking after me.
But it means that I have a sense that no matter what happens, with some limits, I think.
I don't know what it's like to be tortured.

But I have some sense of, even in the midst of a Holocaust, because we read stories of people who have lived through them or met the circumstances, whether they lived through them or not, that they were able to find some sense of a larger, of their life in a larger realm than what comes up in their fears, anxieties, and doubts.
Does that begin to get at Barbara?
**Participant:** The reason I couldn't ask a question earlier is it's very moving and I have a lot of feeling about what you're talking about.
But in John's question, occasionally the people I've met maybe have suffered or pained the most or are able to do it much deeper than I can because they have survived those incidents.
Not all of them, of course, but some who have trusted that they can get really knocked down and get back up are just amazingly trusting, knowing that they've been through that.
If I've been through that, I can be just, you know, whatever comes up, I can do it.

**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** I think, and it's an odd thing to say this to this audience in a way, but I think for people who have not had privilege, who have lived without privilege in a society where they are, in whatever reasons, in whatever way, having to watch their backs, they have to find their own inner sense of who they are and what matters and trust in it, because it's not going to come from the outside.
And when you have been able to get what you want from the outside, your kind of life is reflected back to you.
It's pretty easy.
Even as a woman, my life has been very easy.
It's much harder to find that core, I think.
**Participant:** That also answers my question.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Anyone else before we probably have to finish up?
Well, thank you all very much.
